questions.prompt: What planning reset does Chapter 4 make?
choices: Replace the annual plan as execution master with a 12 week plan
Stop planning until weekly execution improves
Keep the annual plan and add more detail to it

explanation.gentle: The chapter says planning still matters, but the annual plan should no longer govern a 12 week system.
explanation.direct: The authors reject the annual master document and replace it with 12 week planning.
explanation.competitive: The reset is not more paperwork. It is a new execution frame.

questions.prompt: Why does the annual plan fail in this chapter's logic?
choices: It is too short to hold enough goals
It keeps too many priorities open across too much time
It works only for personal goals and not for teams

explanation.gentle: The annual plan stays too broad and too forgiving once execution depends on a shorter cycle.
explanation.direct: The problem is mismatch: the annual structure spreads consequence too far out and preserves overload.
explanation.competitive: It keeps clutter alive by giving it a long horizon to hide inside.

questions.prompt: What makes 12 week planning different from an annual plan with fewer weeks on the page?
choices: It lowers ambition so the cycle feels safer
It changes selectivity and forces narrower goal choice
It removes the need for weekly execution

explanation.gentle: The chapter says a 12 week plan has to be more selective, not just shorter on the calendar.
explanation.direct: The real shift is narrower active commitments and tighter execution pressure.
explanation.competitive: If the plan does not cut scope, it is still the old plan in a smaller box.

questions.prompt: Julian's department plan still carries every major initiative from the year. What Chapter 4 move is strongest?
choices: Keep all initiatives active but track them more closely
Wait for weekly execution to solve the overload later
Reduce the active plan to the few outcomes that deserve the next 12 weeks

explanation.gentle: The chapter says focus improves when the plan stops trying to keep everything alive at once.
explanation.direct: Julian needs selection first, not tighter monitoring of an overloaded plan.
explanation.competitive: A crowded roadmap does not become sharp just because you stare at it harder.

questions.prompt: What distinction does the chapter make between having a plan and having a plan built for execution?
choices: A plan built for execution narrows goals and supports action while the cycle is still alive
A plan built for execution contains more detailed task lists than other plans
A plan built for execution works only in business settings

explanation.gentle: A strong plan helps guide action now instead of simply holding intentions in an organized format.
explanation.direct: Execution design requires selectivity and structure close enough to real work to support correction.
explanation.competitive: The test is whether the plan can run the cycle, not whether it looks complete.

questions.prompt: Which mistake best matches the chapter's overload warning?
choices: Compressing the annual plan into 12 weeks without narrowing scope
Choosing too few goals and revisiting them weekly
Linking vision to the plan before building weekly routines

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that a shorter time frame does not help if the plan still keeps the same overload.
explanation.direct: Compression is not focus. The annual mindset survives whenever scope stays bloated.

questions.prompt: Naomi's semester planner never guided her week when pressure arrived. Which diagnosis fits Chapter 4 best?
choices: She needed a better color-coding system
The plan held too many active aims to function as an execution map
She should have made the semester plan even longer

explanation.gentle: The chapter says a plan can be organized and still be too crowded to guide real action.
explanation.direct: Naomi needed a shorter and more selective planning frame, not more planner detail.
explanation.competitive: The planner stored ambition instead of concentrating pressure.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 4 treat goal selection as part of planning strength?
choices: Because excluding some goals helps execution energy concentrate on the few that matter most
Because fewer goals always mean lower ambition
Because goal selection matters only after weekly planning is complete

explanation.gentle: The chapter says a stronger plan is willing to exclude so the chosen goals can actually govern the cycle.
explanation.direct: Selection is what prevents the 12 week plan from scattering energy across too many commitments.
explanation.competitive: Focus gets force when the plan starts saying no.

questions.prompt: What threshold question sits underneath the chapter's hard warning?
choices: How do I make the annual plan feel more motivational?
When does a 12 week plan become execution architecture instead of compressed overload?
How do I remove all tradeoffs from the cycle before I begin?

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps asking whether the shorter plan truly sharpens action or merely squeezes the same clutter into fewer weeks.
explanation.direct: The hard test is whether the plan narrows scope and supports governable execution.
explanation.competitive: The question is simple: did the reset create focus or just faster chaos?

questions.prompt: If Chapter 4 is right, what should naturally follow once the 12 week plan is selective enough?
choices: A weekly mechanism that keeps the focused plan alive under real demands
A larger annual review to restore every excluded goal
A decision to avoid structure so flexibility stays high

explanation.gentle: The chapter points forward to weekly execution as the way a focused 12 week plan stays active.
explanation.direct: Once the plan has the right structure, the next question is how the week operationalizes it.
explanation.competitive: The next move is not more scope. It is weekly control.
